A sufficient integral condition for local regularity of solutions to the surface growth model

Wojciech S. Ożański
Abstract

The surface growth model, ut+ux​x​x​x+∂x​xux2=0u_{t}+u_{xxxx}+\partial_{xx}u_{x}^{2}=0, is a one-dimensional fourth order equation, which shares a number of striking similarities with the three-dimensional incompressible Navier–Stokes equations, including the results regarding existence and uniqueness of solutions and the partial regularity theory. Here we show that a weak solution of this equation is smooth on a space-time cylinder QQ if the Serrin condition ux∈Lq′​Lq​(Q)u_{x}\in L^{q^{\prime}}L^{q}(Q) is satisfied, where q,q′∈[1,∞]q,q^{\prime}\in[1,\infty] are such that either 1/q+4/q′<11/q+4/q^{\prime}<1 or 1/q+4/q′=11/q+4/q^{\prime}=1, q′<∞q^{\prime}<\infty.

1 Introduction

We consider the one-dimensional model of surface growth

ut+ux​x​x​x+∂x​xux2=0u_{t}+u_{xxxx}+\partial_{xx}u_{x}^{2}=0 (1.1)

on the one-dimensional torus 𝕋{\mathbb{T}}, under the assumption that ∫𝕋u=0\int_{{\mathbb{T}}}u=0. This equation originates from a model of epitaxy, see Siegert & Plischke (1994), Winkler (2011), Stein & Winkler (2005), Cuerno et al. (2005) and Raible et al. (2000) As observed by Blömker & Romito (2009), Blömker & Romito (2012) this model shares many striking similarities with the three-dimensional incompressible Navier–Stokes equations (NSE), including the results regarding existence and uniqueness of solutions. For example their 2009 paper proves local existence in the critical space H˙1/2\dot{H}^{1/2} and (spatial) smoothness for solutions bounded in L8/(2​α−1)​((0,T),Hα)L^{8/(2\alpha-1)}((0,T);H^{\alpha}) for all α∈(1/2,9/2)\alpha\in(1/2,9/2). The 2012 paper proves local existence in a critical space of a similar type to that occurring in the paper by Koch & Tataru (2001) for the NSE. Very recently Ożański & Robinson (2017) developed a partial regularity theory for the surface growth model, an analogue of the celebrated Caffarelli et al. (1982) theorem for the NSE. The central result of this theory is that there exists ε0>0\varepsilon_{0}>0 such any “suitable” weak solution of the surface growth model (see Definition 2.5) satisfying

1r2​∫Q⁡(z,r)|ux|3<ε0\frac{1}{r^{2}}\int_{Q(z,r)}|u_{x}|^{3}<\varepsilon_{0} (1.2)

is Hölder continuous (with any exponent α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1)) in Q⁡(z,r/2)Q(z,r/2) (see Theorem 4.5 in Ożański & Robinson (2017)). Here Q⁡(z,r)Q(z,r) denotes a space-time cylinder of radius rr centred at zz and “suitable” refers to weak solutions satisfying a local form of an energy inequality, see Ożański & Robinson (2017) for precise definitions. A straightforward consequence of this result is that one can estimate the dimension of the singular set

S:={(x,t)∈𝕋×[0,∞):u is not space-time Hölder continuousin any neighbourhood of (x,t)}.\begin{split}S&:=\{(x,t)\in{\mathbb{T}}\times[0,\infty):\ u\mbox{ is not space-time H\"{o}lder continuous}\\ &\hskip 128.0374pt\qquad\qquad\qquad\mbox{in any neighbourhood of }(x,t)\}.\end{split} (1.3)

Namely one obtains dB​(S)≤7/6d_{B}(S)\leq 7/6, where dBd_{B} denotes the box-counting dimension. Another consequence of the partial regularity theory is that dH​(S)≤1d_{H}(S)\leq 1, where dHd_{H} denotes the Hausdorff dimension.

Unfortunately it is not known whether the definition (1.3) of the singular set is optimal; that is whether uu is smooth (locally) outside SS.

Interestingly, it seems that the proof of the partial regularity theory cannot be obtained by the method of Caffarelli et al. (1982); instead Ożański & Robinson (2017) used the approach of Lin (1998) and Ladyzhenskaya & Seregin (1999); the analysis there also required a novel tool, namely a nonlinear parabolic Poincaré inequality,

1r5​∫Q⁡(z,r/2)|u−uz,r/2|3≤Cp​p​(Y⁡(z,r)+Y​(z,r)2),\frac{1}{r^{5}}\int_{Q(z,r/2)}|u-u_{z,r/2}|^{3}\leq C_{pp}\left({\rm Y}(z,r)+{\rm Y}(z,r)^{2}\right), (1.4)

for weak solutions of the surface growth model, where

Y⁡(z,r):=1r2​∫Q⁡(z,r)|ux|3{\rm Y}(z,r):=\frac{1}{r^{2}}\int_{Q(z,r)}|u_{x}|^{3}

and uz,r/2u_{z,r/2} denotes the mean of uu over Q⁡(z,r/2)Q(z,r/2).

In this article we study another property of weak solutions of the surface growth model, which is similar to the so-called local Serrin condition in the case of the Navier–Stokes equations. In the case of the NSE this condition reads: if uu is a weak solution on a space-time domain U×(t1,t2)U\times(t_{1},t_{2}) such that

u∈Lq′​((t1,t2),Lq​(U)) with ​3q+2q′≤1u\in L^{q^{\prime}}((t_{1},t_{2});L^{q}(U))\quad\text{ with }\frac{3}{q}+\frac{2}{q^{\prime}}\leq 1 (1.5)

then uu is smooth in the space variables on this domain. The condition is named after Serrin (1962 & 1963), who was the first to study the property (1.5) in the subcritical case (that is when the inequality in (1.5) is sharp “<<”). The critical case (that is when 2/q′+3/q=12/q^{\prime}+3/q=1) has been studied by Fabes et al. (1972) when q∈(3,∞)q\in(3,\infty), and Struwe (1988), Takahashi (1990) when q>3q>3. The most difficult case of q′=∞,q=3q^{\prime}=\infty,q=3 was resolved by Escauriaza, Seregin & Šverák (2003). We refer the reader to an excellent presentation of the local Serrin condition in the NSE and further references in Chapter 13 of Robinson et al. (2016).

Here, we prove that a weak solution uu to the surface growth model on a space-time domain U×(t1,t2)U\times(t_{1},t_{2}) is smooth on this domain provided that

ux∈Lq′​((t1,t2),Lq​(U)) where 1q+4q′≤1u_{x}\in L^{q^{\prime}}((t_{1},t_{2});L^{q}(U))\quad\text{ where }\quad\frac{1}{q}+\frac{4}{q^{\prime}}\leq 1 (1.6)

(and q,q′∈(1,∞]q,q^{\prime}\in(1,\infty]), see Theorem 3.1 for the subcritical case (i.e. 1/q+4/q′<11/q+4/q^{\prime}<1) and Theorem 3.2 for the critical case (i.e. 1/q+4/q′=11/q+4/q^{\prime}=1). Remarkably, under this condition we obtain smoothness in both space and time (rather than smoothness in space only, as in the case of the NSE). Note that from all possible choices of the exponents q,q′q,q^{\prime} satisfying the relation in (1.6) we only exclude the choice q=1q=1, q′=∞q^{\prime}=\infty (see the conclusion for a discussion regarding this case). Moreover observe that we state the Serrin condition (1.6) in terms of uxu_{x} (rather than in terms of uu, which is the case in the NSE). This is related to the fact that the lowest spatial derivative of uu involved in the nonlinear term in the surface growth model (1.1) is uxu_{x} (rather than the 00-th derivative, which is the case in the NSE). Note that the condition for local regularity from Ożański & Robinson (2017) is also stated in terms of uxu_{x} (see (1.2)). Therefore, our main result is a next step towards understanding the remarkable similarity between the SGM and the NSE.

Interestingly, local Hölder continuity of uu follows trivially from the subcritical Serrin condition by a use of an extended version of the parabolic Poincaré inequality. Indeed the parabolic Poincaré inequality (1.4) can be extended to

1r5​∫Q⁡(z0,r/2)|u−uz0,r/2|p≤C⁡((rε​M)p+(rε​M)2​p),\frac{1}{r^{5}}\int_{Q(z_{0},r/2)}|u-u_{z_{0},r/2}|^{p}\leq C\left((r^{\varepsilon}M)^{p}+(r^{\varepsilon}M)^{2p}\right), (1.7)

where

M:=[∫t1t2(∫U|ux​(t)|p)p′/p​𝑑t]1/p′M:=\left[\int_{t_{1}}^{t_{2}}\left(\int_{U}|u_{x}(t)|^{p}\right)^{p^{\prime}/p}{\rm d}t\right]^{1/p^{\prime}}

and p,p′∈[2,∞)p,p^{\prime}\in[2,\infty) are such that 1/p+4/p′=1−ε1/p+4/p^{\prime}=1-\varepsilon. Such an extension can be proved in the same way as (1.4) (see Theorem 3.1 in Ożański & Robinson (2017)). Thus if the condition (1.6) is satisfied with 1/q+4/q′=1−ε1/q+4/q^{\prime}=1-\varepsilon, then an application of Hölder’s inequality to (1.7) together with the Campanato lemma give ε\varepsilon-Hölder continuity of uu in U×(t1,t2)U\times(t_{1},t_{2}).

What is more, in the same circumstances (and also allowing the case 1/q+4/q′=11/q+4/q^{\prime}=1, q′<∞q^{\prime}<\infty) the partial regularity theory gives α\alpha-Hölder continuity for any α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1) if q≥3q\geq 3. Indeed, Hölder’s inequality gives

1r2​∫Q⁡(z,r)|ux|3≤‖ux‖Lq′,q​(Q​(z,r))3​r3​(1−1/q−4/q′),\frac{1}{r^{2}}\int_{Q(z,r)}|u_{x}|^{3}\leq\|u_{x}\|^{3}_{L^{q^{\prime},q}(Q(z,r))}r^{3(1-1/q-4/q^{\prime})},

which is less than ε0\varepsilon_{0} if the cylinder Q⁡(z,r)Q(z,r) is small enough (provided q′<∞q^{\prime}<\infty, which can be guaranteed in any case, cf. the beginning of the proof of Theorem 3.1). Thus the condition (1.2) for partial regularity can be guaranteed for each sufficiently small cylinder Q⁡(z,r)Q(z,r), and the claim follows. Therefore the main result of this article is interesting, since it shows that the local Serrin condition (1.6) gives C∞C^{\infty} smoothness, rather than merely α\alpha-Hölder continuity for any α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1). This also suggests that the definition of the singular set (1.3) is optimal.

The proof of our result begins with the approach of Takahashi (1990), adapted to the one-dimensional fourth order setting. However, in order to show boundedness of higher derivatives in space, we use fractional order Sobolev spaces to obtain, roughly speaking, a half of a derivative at a time (see step 2’ of the proof of Theorem 3.1). This seems to be a novel approach in this context. Moreover, our setting requires a uniqueness theorem for weak solutions of the biharmonic heat equation wt+wx​x​x​x=0w_{t}+w_{xxxx}=0. Since we are dealing with a fourth order equation, we cannot adapt any uniqueness theorem for the heat equation which uses the maximum principle. We can, however, adapt a uniqueness theorem for the heat equation which is based on the density of the image of the heat operator ∂t−Δ\partial_{t}-\Delta in LpL^{p}. A uniqueness theorem of this kind is presented in Section 4.4.2 of Giga et al. (2010) and we prove an appropriate adaptation of it in Theorem 2.4 below.

The structure of the article is the following. In Section 2 we discuss the preliminary concepts including fractional Sobolev spaces (Section 2.1), the biharmonic heat kernel (Section 2.2), the uniqueness theorem (Section 2.3) and the concept of local weak solutions to the surface growth model (Section 2.4). We then proceed to the proof of the local Serrin condition for the surface growth model in Section 3. There, we discuss a certain representation formula for uxu_{x} and we prove regularity, first for the subcritical case 1/q+4/q′<11/q+4/q^{\prime}<1 in Section 3.1 and then for the critical case 1/q+4/q′=11/q+4/q^{\prime}=1 with q′<∞q^{\prime}<\infty in Section 3.2.

We will write ∂t\partial_{t} for the derivative in time and ∂x\partial_{x} for the derivative in xx. We say that a function satisfies a partial differential equation in an open set if it satisfies the distributional form of the equation. We denote a space-time cylinder by QQ, that is Q=B×IQ=B\times I for some intervals B,I⊂ℝB,I\subset\mathbb{R}. where

‖f‖Lp′,p​(Q)p′:=∫I‖f⁡(t)‖Lp​(B)p′​𝑑t\|f\|_{L^{p^{\prime},p}(Q)}^{p^{\prime}}:=\int_{I}\|f(t)\|_{L^{p}(B)}^{p^{\prime}}{\rm d}t

for p′<∞p^{\prime}<\infty and

‖f‖L∞,p​(Q):=esssupt∈I​‖f⁡(t)‖Lp​(B).\|f\|_{L^{\infty,p}(Q)}:=\mathrm{esssup}_{t\in I}\|f(t)\|_{L^{p}(B)}.

Given T>0T>0 we use the shorthand notation Lp′,p:=Lp′,p​(ℝ×(0,T))L^{p^{\prime},p}:=L^{p^{\prime},p}(\mathbb{R}\times(0,T)) and ∥⋅∥p′,p:=∥⋅∥Lp′,p​(ℝ×(0,T))\|\cdot\|_{p^{\prime},p}:=\|\cdot\|_{L^{p^{\prime},p}(\mathbb{R}\times(0,T))}. (2003) corresponds to L∞,3L^{\infty,3} in our notation.

2.3 Uniqueness of solutions to homogeneous biharmonic heat equation

Theorem 2.4 (Uniqueness of solutions to homogeneous biharmonic heat equation).

Suppose that q,q′∈[1,∞]q,q^{\prime}\in[1,\infty] and v∈Lq′,qv\in L^{q^{\prime},q} is a distributional solution to the homogeneous biharmonic heat equation, that is

We modify the argument from Section 4.4.2 of Giga et al. (2010). We focus on the case T<∞T<\infty (the case T=∞T=\infty follows trivially by applying the result for all T>0T>0).

We first observe that the assumption v∈Lq′,qv\in L^{q^{\prime},q} implies that (2.13) holds also for all ϕ∈C∞​(ℝ×[0,T))\phi\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}\times[0,T)) such that

{∂tk∂xmϕ∈Lp′,pfor every ​k,m≥0,supp​ϕ⊂ℝ×[0,T′) for some ​T′<T,\begin{cases}\partial_{t}^{k}\partial_{x}^{m}\phi\in L^{p^{\prime},p}&\text{for every }k,m\geq 0,\\ \mathrm{supp}\,\phi\subset\mathbb{R}\times[0,T^{\prime})&\text{ for some }T^{\prime}<T,\end{cases} (2.14)

where 1/p+1/q=11/p+1/q=1, 1/p′+1/q′=11/{p^{\prime}}+1/{q^{\prime}}=1. Indeed, given such ϕ\phi one can consider

ϕj​(x,t):=θj​(x)​ϕ​(x,t),\phi_{j}(x,t):=\theta_{j}(x)\phi(x,t),

where θj​(x):=θ⁡(x/j)\theta_{j}(x):=\theta(x/j) and θ∈C∞​(ℝ,[0,1])\theta\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R};[0,1]) is any function such that θ⁡(τ)=1\theta(\tau)=1 for |τ|≤1|\tau|\leq 1 and θ⁡(τ)=0\theta(\tau)=0 for τ≥2\tau\geq 2. Then ϕj\phi_{j} can be used as a test function in (2.13) and a simple use of the Dominated Convergence Theorem together with the properties (2.14) and the assumption v∈Lq′,qv\in L^{q^{\prime},q} proves the claim.

We will show that

∫0T∫v​Ψ=0\int_{0}^{T}\int v\Psi=0

Given Ψ∈C0∞​(ℝ3×(0,T))\Psi\in C_{0}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{3}\times(0,T)) let T′<TT^{\prime}<T be such that Ψ⁡(t)≡0\Psi(t)\equiv 0 for t≥T′t\geq T^{\prime}. Extend Ψ\Psi by zero for t≤0t\leq 0 and t≥Tt\geq T. Let

where Φ\Phi denotes the biharmonic heat kernel (see (2.4)). Then ϕ\phi solves the biharmonic heat equation backwards from TT with right-hand side Ψ\Psi, that is

{ϕt−ϕx​x​x​x=Ψ in ​ℝ×(−∞,T),ϕ⁡(T)=0.\begin{cases}\phi_{t}-\phi_{xxxx}=\Psi\qquad\text{ in }\mathbb{R}\times(-\infty,T),\\ \phi(T)=0.\end{cases} (2.15)

In fact, we have ϕ⁡(t)=0\phi(t)=0 for t∈[T′,T]t\in[T^{\prime},T]. By the biharmonic heat estimates (see (2.5)) we see that ϕ\phi satisfies (2.14). Thus (2.13) gives

0=∫0T∫v⁡(ϕt−ϕx​x​x​x)=∫0T∫v​Ψ,0=\int_{0}^{T}\int v(\phi_{t}-\phi_{xxxx})=\int_{0}^{T}\int v\Psi,

as required. ∎

2.4 Weak solutions of the surface growth model

Here we define the notion of a weak solution to the surface growth model. Since the local Serrin condition is concerned with behaviour of weak solutions in bounded cylinders in space-time, we focus only on the notion of a local solution (in space-time; rather than a solution to the initial value problem).

Definition 2.5 (Weak solution of the SGM).

We say that u∈L∞,2​(Q)u\in L^{\infty,2}(Q) is a weak solution of the surface growth model on a cylinder QQ if ux​x∈L2,2​(Q)u_{xx}\in L^{2,2}(Q) and

∫Q(u​ϕt−ux​x​ϕx​x−ux2​ϕx​x)=0\int_{Q}\left(u\,\phi_{t}-u_{xx}\phi_{xx}-u_{x}^{2}\phi_{xx}\right)=0

for all ϕ∈C0∞​(Q)\phi\in C_{0}^{\infty}(Q).

In what follows we will assume that uu is a weak solution of the SGM on a given QQ. Note that any weak solution uu on a cylinder QQ satisfies

ux∈L10/3,10/3​(Q)u_{x}\in L^{10/3,10/3}(Q) (2.16)

(which can be shown using Sobolev interpolation; see (2.5) in Ożański & Robinson (2017) for details), and so in particular the integral in the equation above is well-defined. Moreover

ux∈L16/3,2​(Q),u_{x}\in L^{16/3,2}(Q), (2.17)

given the main assumption of this article (i.e. (1.6)) is satisfied with q∈(1,2]q\in(1,2], which follows by a simple application of Lebesgue interpolation (in space and then in time) between (2.16) and (1.6). We will need (2.17) in order to circumvent a certain technical issue in the proof of the main result when q∈(1,2]q\in(1,2] (see the comments following (3.7) for details).

3.1 The subcritical case

Here we focus on the subcritical case, namely the first case of (3.1).

Theorem 3.1 (Local Serrin condition, subcritical case).

Let uu be a weak solution to the surface growth model on a cylinder QQ and let q,q′∈(1,∞]q,q^{\prime}\in(1,\infty] satisfy 1/q+4/q′<11/q+4/q^{\prime}<1. If

First, by translation we can assume that QQ is contained within a time interval (0,T)(0,T) for some T>0T>0; that is Q⋐ℝ×(0,T)Q\Subset\mathbb{R}\times(0,T).

Secondly we can assume that q′<∞q^{\prime}<\infty. Indeed, since the choice of the exponents q′,qq^{\prime},q is subcritical, the case q′=∞q^{\prime}=\infty can be reduced to q′<∞q^{\prime}<\infty by a use of Hölder’s inequality,

‖ux‖Lq′,q​(Q)≤C​‖ux‖L∞,q​(Q),\|u_{x}\|_{L^{q^{\prime},q}(Q)}\leq C\|u_{x}\|_{L^{\infty,q}(Q)},

where q′<∞q^{\prime}<\infty is sufficiently large such that 1/q+4/q′<11/q+4/q^{\prime}<1 holds.

Thirdly it suffices to prove the result under a smallness condition

‖ux‖Lq′,q​(Q)≤δ\|u_{x}\|_{L^{q^{\prime},q}(Q)}\leq\delta (3.5)

for δ>0\delta>0 sufficiently small such that

The proof of the result proceeds in a few steps.

Step 1. Show that ux∈L∞​(Q~)u_{x}\in L^{\infty}(\widetilde{Q}) for any Q~⋐Q\widetilde{Q}\Subset Q.

‖w‖∞,∞≤Cq,q′,∞,∞​‖w​v‖q′,q+C⁡(‖v2‖Lq′/2,q/2​(Q)+‖v‖Lq′,q​(Q))\|w\|_{\infty,\infty}\leq C_{q,q^{\prime},\infty,\infty}\|wv\|_{q^{\prime},q}+C\left(\|v^{2}\|_{L^{q^{\prime}/2,q/2}(Q)}+\|v\|_{L^{q^{\prime},q}(Q)}\right) (3.7)

Step 3. Deduce the smoothness of uu.

From the surface growth equation, ut+ux​x​x​x+∂x​xux2=0u_{t}+u_{xxxx}+\partial_{xx}u_{x}^{2}=0, and steps 1 and 2 we see that utu_{t} (in the sense of weak derivatives) is bounded on every compact subset of QQ. Similarly every derivative (in both xx and tt) is bounded on every compact subset of QQ. Thus the Rellich–Kondrachov embedding (see, for example, Theorem 6.3 in Adams & Fournier (2003)) gives smoothness of uu in QQ.∎

3.2 The critical case

We now focus on the critical case, namely the second case of (3.1).

Theorem 3.2 (Local Serrin condition, critical case).

Let uu be a weak solution to the surface growth model on a cylinder QQ and let q,q′∈(1,∞]q,q^{\prime}\in(1,\infty] satisfy 1/q+4/q′=11/q+4/q^{\prime}=1. If

ux∈Lq′,q​(Q)u_{x}\in L^{q^{\prime},q}(Q)

then u∈C∞​(Q)u\in C^{\infty}(Q).

Proof.

Similarly as in Theorem 3.1 we can assume that Q⋐ℝ×(0,T)Q\Subset\mathbb{R}\times(0,T) and we can assume the smallness condition (3.5), since q′<∞q^{\prime}<\infty.

Let Q~⋐Q\widetilde{Q}\Subset Q and fix p′∈(q′,∞)p^{\prime}\in(q^{\prime},\infty), p∈(q,∞)p\in(q,\infty) satisfying 1/p+4/p′<11/p+4/p^{\prime}<1. We will show that ux∈Lp′,p​(Q~)u_{x}\in L^{p^{\prime},p}(\widetilde{Q}) (then the claim follows from Theorem 3.1).

As in the proof of Theorem 3.1 let v:=uxv:=u_{x}, ϕ∈C0∞​(Q,[0,1])\phi\in C_{0}^{\infty}(Q;[0,1]) be such that ϕ=1\phi=1 on Q~\widetilde{Q}. As in (3.4) w:=v​ϕw:=v\phi satisfies the representation (3.4),

w(t)=−∫0tΦx​x​x(t−s)∗[w(s)v(s)]ds+∫0tΦ(t−s)∗fv(s)ds.w(t)=-\int_{0}^{t}\Phi_{xxx}(t-s)\ast\left[w(s)v(s)\right]{\rm d}s+\int_{0}^{t}\Phi(t-s)\ast f_{v}(s)\,{\rm d}s. (3.21)

Corollary 2.2 applied with r=pr=p, r′=p′r^{\prime}=p^{\prime} gives

‖w‖p′,p≤Cl,l′,p,p′​‖w​v‖l′,l+C⁡(‖v2‖Lq′/2,q/2​(Q)+‖v‖Lq′,q​(Q)),\|w\|_{p^{\prime},p}\leq C_{l,l^{\prime},p,p^{\prime}}\|wv\|_{l^{\prime},l}+C\left(\|v^{2}\|_{L^{q^{\prime}/2,q/2}(Q)}+\|v\|_{L^{q^{\prime},q}(Q)}\right), (3.22)

where 1/l=1/p+1/q1/l=1/p+1/q, 1/l′=1/p′+1/q′1/l^{\prime}=1/p^{\prime}+1/q^{\prime} (note l∈(q,p)l\in(q,p), l′∈(q′,p′)l^{\prime}\in(q^{\prime},p^{\prime})), cf. (3.7). (Note that again we have implicitly assumed that q>2q>2, see the section below for the case q∈(1,2]q\in(1,2].) Applying Hölder’s inequality to first term on the right-hand side of (3.22) and using the smallness condition (3.5) with δ<1/2​Cl,l′,p,p′\delta<1/2C_{l,l^{\prime},p,p^{\prime}} gives

‖w‖p′,p≤12​‖w‖p′,p+C⁡(‖v‖Lq′,q​(Q)2+‖v‖Lq′,q​(Q))\|w\|_{p^{\prime},p}\leq\frac{1}{2}\|w\|_{p^{\prime},p}+C\left(\|v\|_{L^{q^{\prime},q}(Q)}^{2}+\|v\|_{L^{q^{\prime},q}(Q)}\right) (3.23)

Thus, subtracting the first term on the right hand side we obtain w∈Lp′,p​(Q)w\in L^{p^{\prime},p}(Q), which gives in particular that v∈Lp′,p​(Q~)v\in L^{p^{\prime},p}(\widetilde{Q}), as required.

Note that, similarly as in step 1 of the proof of Theorem 3.1, this subtraction requires a rigorous justification, and can be verified similarly as in step 1’ of that proof. ∎

3.3 The case q∈(1,2]q\in(1,2]

Here we briefly show that if q,q′q,q^{\prime} satisfy q∈(1,2]q\in(1,2] and 1/q+4/q′≤11/q+4/q^{\prime}\leq 1 then one can apply a similar argument as in (3.22) to obtain that v∈Lp′,p​(Q′)v\in L^{p^{\prime},p}(Q^{\prime}) for p=2p=2, any p′∈(max⁡(q′,8/3),∞)p^{\prime}\in(\max(q^{\prime},8/3),\infty) and any subcylinder Q′⋐QQ^{\prime}\Subset Q. Note that, since 1/p+4/p′<11/p+4/p^{\prime}<1, the claim (i.e. ux∈C∞​(Q)u_{x}\in C^{\infty}(Q)) then follows by Theorem 3.1.

In order to show that v∈Lp′,p​(Q′)v\in L^{p^{\prime},p}(Q^{\prime}) observe that the last term of (3.21) can be bounded in the Lp′,pL^{p^{\prime},p} norm by

C⁡(‖v2‖L8/3,1​(Q)+‖v‖Lq′,q​(Q)),C\left(\|v^{2}\|_{L^{8/3,1}(Q)}+\|v\|_{L^{q^{\prime},q}(Q)}\right),

where we used Corollary 2.2 again (recall that v∈L16/3,2​(Q)v\in L^{16/3,2}(Q) (see (2.17)) and observe that the choice of exponents r′=p′r^{\prime}=p^{\prime}, r=2r=2, l′=8/3l^{\prime}=8/3, l=1l=1 satisfies (2.8) with k=2k=2). Thus (3.22) follows as in the proof above with ‖v2‖Lq′/2,q/2​(Q)\|v^{2}\|_{L^{q^{\prime}/2,q/2}(Q)} replaced by ‖v2‖L8/3,1​(Q)\|v^{2}\|_{L^{8/3,1}(Q)}. As in (3.23) we arrive at

‖w‖p′,p≤12​‖w‖p′,p+C⁡(‖v‖L16/3,2​(Q)2+‖v‖Lq′,q​(Q)),\|w\|_{p^{\prime},p}\leq\frac{1}{2}\|w\|_{p^{\prime},p}+C\left(\|v\|_{L^{16/3,2}(Q)}^{2}+\|v\|_{L^{q^{\prime},q}(Q)}\right),

from which we deduce that v∈Lp′,p​(Q~)v\in L^{p^{\prime},p}(\widetilde{Q}) for any Q~⋐Q\widetilde{Q}\Subset Q (as in the proof above; namely by regularising the equation and taking a limit as in step 1’ of the proof of Theorem 3.1).

Finally, observe that the issue discussed in this section does not appear in the case of the Navier–Stokes equation. In fact, in the case of the NSE the dimension of space is larger that the order of the nonlinearity (i.e. 22); to be more precise the constraint of the exponents 2/q′+3/q≤12/q^{\prime}+3/q\leq 1 (recall (1.5)) implies q≥3>2q\geq 3>2.

Conclusion

We have proved that a weak solution to the surface growth model (1.1) on a cylinder QQ is smooth if it satisfies the local Serrin condition u∈Lq′,q​(Q)u\in L^{q^{\prime},q}(Q) where q∈[2,∞]q\in[2,\infty], q′∈[4,∞]q^{\prime}\in[4,\infty] are such that either 1/q+4/q′<11/q+4/q^{\prime}<1 or 1/q+4/q′=11/q+4/q^{\prime}=1, q′<∞q^{\prime}<\infty. Our analysis excludes the endpoint case q=1q=1, q′=∞q^{\prime}=\infty since in this case we cannot assume the smallness condition (3.5). This case is not only particularly interesting, but also particularly challenging. In fact, the analogous problem in the case of the NSE is the problem whether a weak solution u∈L∞,3​(Q)u\in L^{\infty,3}(Q) to the NSE on QQ is regular in QQ, and it was resolved in a deep paper by Escauriaza et al. (2003) using a blow-up technique. We believe that, despite the fact that the SGM is a one-dimensional equation, it might be a more difficult problem than in the case of the NSE, since a number of techniques used by Escauriaza et al. (2003) seem unavailable in the SGM (such as the Ls,lL_{s,l}-coercive estimates for solutions of the non-stationary Stokes system) and since the L1L^{1} space is not reflexive.

However, given the number of similarities between the SGM and the NSE, as developed in the recent years, it is expected that the case q=1q=1, q′=∞q^{\prime}=\infty gives regularity as well.
